drills.q: Why is SSE the dominant transport for LLM token streaming instead of WebSockets, and when would you actually pick WebSockets instead?
drills.a: Token streaming is one-directional; SSE over HTTP is stateless per-request, scales horizontally without sticky sessions, and works through standard proxies/load balancers/CDNs. WebSockets earn their keep only when the client must send data mid-stream: voice-agent barge-in, a mid-generation approval gate, or true multi-user collaboration.

drills.q: Why can't you use the browser's native EventSource API for an authenticated LLM chat endpoint, and what do you use instead?
drills.a: EventSource only supports GET with no custom headers and no body, so it can't send the message history (POST body) or an Authorization header. Use fetch() with a ReadableStream reader, decoding chunks with TextDecoder and manually parsing SSE frame boundaries (split on \n\n).

drills.q: Your chat UI stutters badly with a fast model but is smooth with a slow one. Diagnose and fix it.
drills.a: Per-token setState triggers a re-render; if the render tree does expensive work (markdown parse, syntax highlight) and the model emits tokens faster than that completes within a 16.7ms frame budget, the main thread falls behind. Fix: buffer incoming deltas and flush on requestAnimationFrame, and move expensive rendering off the synchronous per-chunk path.

drills.q: SSE has no backpressure mechanism. What does that mean precisely, and does it actually matter for plain text token streaming?
drills.a: The server has no signal the client is falling behind and the client has no way to say "slow down" -- unlike WebSockets (bufferedAmount, TCP receive window). Rarely matters for small text payloads, but matters if something heavier rides the stream (large tool results, base64 chunks); mitigate at the application layer (chunk payloads, defer expensive rendering), not by switching transports.

drills.q: Walk through what actually happens end-to-end when a user clicks Stop mid-generation, and how you'd verify it's wired correctly.
drills.a: controller.abort() rejects the fetch promise (AbortError, expected) and closes the TCP connection, firing a close event on the server's request object. Generation only actually stops if the server explicitly listens for that close event and cancels the upstream LLM call there. Verify by aborting a test stream partway through and checking the provider's usage/billing metrics reflect a truncated, not full, generation.

drills.q: Design the state shape for a chat message with interleaved text and tool calls, and explain how to avoid the tool-call card remounting when its result arrives.
drills.a: A message is { id, role, parts: [...] } with typed entries (text, tool-call, tool-result) in order, not a single string. Avoid remount/flash by keying state by toolCallId and updating the existing part in place when the result arrives, rather than appending a second separate entry.

drills.q: A streamed response arrives all at once instead of incrementally, though the server writes incrementally. Diagnose and fix, and describe how you'd catch this in CI.
drills.a: Likely cause: a reverse proxy (commonly nginx) buffering the response by default. Fix: disable buffering for the route (X-Accel-Buffering: no / proxy_buffering off), verify with curl -N directly against the endpoint. Catch in CI with an integration test against the actual deployed proxy config asserting chunks arrive with measurable gaps, not just testing the app server directly.

drills.q: Why send periodic heartbeat comment lines during a long tool call with no token output, and does this affect billing?
drills.a: Load balancers/proxies with idle-connection timeouts (commonly 30-60s) can't distinguish silent-but-working from dead and will kill the connection. A ": ping\n\n" comment line every ~15s (ignored by the client's event parser since it has no data: field) keeps it alive. No billing impact -- it's a transport-level liveness signal, not part of model output.

drills.q: Why is TextDecoder's { stream: true } option necessary for consuming a chunked stream, and why wouldn't typical English test fixtures catch its absence?
drills.a: Multi-byte UTF-8 characters (emoji, CJK) can split across chunk boundaries; without stream:true each decode() call treats input as complete and corrupts an incomplete trailing sequence into a replacement character. Plain ASCII test fixtures never exercise this since every character is one byte -- catching it requires fixtures with multi-byte characters positioned near expected chunk boundaries.

drills.q: Design resumable streaming for a user whose connection drops mid-generation on a flaky mobile network.
drills.a: Server persists generated content against a stream/request id as it's produced. Client tracks the last received position (cursor/offset or SSE id). On reconnect, client sends that cursor; server replays already-generated content instantly from its persisted buffer, then continues new generation. If the model itself can't resume mid-generation, the honest fallback is a clear "regenerate from here" UI affordance rather than a silent, confusing partial state.

drills.q: What determines token arrival rate at the systems level, and how would you find the real number for a given deployment rather than assuming a constant?
drills.a: Model size, batch size/concurrency on the serving side, hardware, and decoding strategy (e.g. speculative decoding) determine it -- it's not frontend-controlled and varies by provider/tier/load. Instrument the client to log timestamped delta arrivals, compute inter-arrival intervals under realistic concurrent load, and design buffering against the observed p95, not an unloaded local test.

drills.q: What structurally changed in Vercel AI SDK v6 (May 2026) versus v5, and why is it called a "silent" breaking change?
drills.a: useChat's message shape moved to an interleaved parts model (text-delta/tool-call/tool-result/reasoning as an ordered array), the tool-call streaming lifecycle gained explicit step hooks, and the wire format changed. It's silent because old v5 code keeps compiling against the new v6 message shape -- it's a structural shape change, not a renamed export that would fail to build -- so v5 and v6 cannot be mixed in one render tree.
